assignment: When people ask for advice, they sometimes talk to more than one person. Explain why seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice. Use specific details and examples in your response.
essay_1:
More Than One Voice

Last spring my cousin Dana had to decide if she should take a job in a different city. The first person she asked was her mom, and her mom said to stay close to home. If Dana had stopped there she would of said no to the job. But she didn't stop, she kept asking people. She talked to four people total and changed her mind two times before she finally picked. I was around for most of it and it made me think that asking a few people for advice is better than asking only one.

My first reason is that each person only knows part of what is going on. Dana's mom kept talking about how lonely it is in a new city. She moved one time when she was younger and hated it, so thats what she thinks about. Dana's old manager talked about the money and the job title because that is the stuff he knows. Then Dana had a friend who already lived in that city, and she told her about the rent and the traffic and how long it took her to make friends there. Nobody was wrong. But nobody knew everything either. When Dana put all the answers together it was kind of like a map that was almost finished. One person can only give you one piece of the map. When you ask a bunch of people you get the pieces you couldn't see by yourself.

My second reason is that people want things for themselves, even people who love you. Dana's mom wanted her to live nearby. That is a nice thing to want, but it is not the same as what is best for Dana's job. It's like when you go to buy a phone and the guy at the store tells you which one to get. He might be telling the truth, but he also gets paid more if you buy it. If he is the only one you ask, you can't tell which part is real advice and which part is him wanting money. But if you also ask a friend who has that phone, and you look up what somebody who fixes phones says, then it kind of evens out. If three people who all want different things tell you the same answer, you can trust it a lot more than just one of them.

My third reason is that it actually helps when people disagree. This one sounds weird but it's true. Two people Dana really respected told her opposite things, so she had to figure out why. It turned out her manager thought she wanted to move up fast at work, and her friend thought she cared more about having free time. That made Dana ask herself something she never asked before, which was what does she even want for the next five years. Doctors do this too. When somebody needs surgery, a lot of times they get told to go get a second opinion from another doctor. If the second doctor agrees, the person feels better about it. If the second doctor doesn't agree, then the person knows it's not as simple as it sounded, and I would want to know that before they cut me open.

Some people might say that asking too many people just makes you confused. That is true sometimes. Ten opinions could be worse than two, and some people keep asking just so they don't have to decide. But you are not supposed to count votes like an election. Dana didn't take the job because three out of four people said to. She took it because all that talking showed her what she cared about and what could go wrong. Then she picked for herself.

In conclusion, asking more than one person doesn't mean other people decide for you. It gives you more facts and better questions to think about, and it keeps one person from pushing you their way. Dana has lived in her new city for eight months now and she likes it. She still calls her mom every Sunday.
essay_2:
More Than One Voice

Last spring my cousin Dana had to decide if she should take a job in another city. She asked her mom first, and her mom told her to stay close to home. If Dana had stopped there, she would have said no to the job. Instead she kept asking. She talked to four different people, and she changed her mind twice before she picked an answer. Watching her do that showed me why asking a few people for advice is a better way to make a choice than asking just one.

The first reason is that every person only sees part of the picture. Dana's mom thought about how lonely a new city can feel, because she moved once herself and hated it. Dana's old manager thought about the pay and the title, because that is what he knows. A friend who already lived in that city talked about rent, traffic, and how long it took her to meet people. Each of them was right about one piece. When Dana put all their answers side by side, she had something like a whole map. One person gives you one angle. A few people show you the corners you could not see from where you were standing.

The second reason is that people want things for themselves too. Dana's mom wanted her nearby. That is not a bad thing for a mom to want, but it is a different thing from what helps Dana's career. Here is another example. A salesman at the store tells you which phone to buy. He might be honest, but he also gets paid when you buy it. If you only ask him, you have no way to tell where his advice stops and his paycheck starts. So you also ask a friend who owns the phone, and you read what a repair guy says about it. When three people who want different things all say the same thing, you can trust it more.

Third, it helps when people disagree. Two people Dana respected gave her opposite answers, so she had to figure out why. Her manager thought she wanted to move up fast. Her friend thought she cared most about free time. That showed Dana a question she had skipped. What did she want out of the next five years? Doctors know this already. People who need surgery are told to get a second opinion. If the second doctor agrees, the patient goes in calm. If the second doctor says something else, the patient learns there is more to think about, and it is better to know that before anyone picks up a scalpel.

Of course, you can ask too many people. Ten opinions can leave you more mixed up than two, and at some point you are just putting off the choice. The answer is to listen and then think, instead of counting votes. Dana took the job, and it was her own choice. The talks showed her what mattered to her and what could go wrong, and then she chose for herself.

Asking a lot of people still leaves the choice in your own hands. It just gives you more to work with. You get more facts, you get a check on what one person wants, and you get questions you would have missed. It does not make the choice easy, and it does not promise that things will turn out right. Dana has lived in her new city for eight months now. She likes her job, but the first winter was hard and she still gets lonely on weekends. She says she would have been angry at herself if she had only listened to one person, because then she would never have known what she was giving up. She still calls her mom every Sunday. When I have to make a big choice someday, I am going to ask more than one person before I decide.
